### Purpose
The contribution aims to eliminate the high computational cost of solving ODEs during Flow Matching sampling and achieve one-step generation from the initial distribution to the target distribution. Papers [3], [6], [7], [8], [9], [16], [17], [22], and [26] all address the problem of reducing computational overhead in generative models, particularly diffusion or flow-based models, by enabling faster sampling or one-step generation. For example, [6] explicitly discusses distilling diffusion models into one-step generators to reduce computational demands, and [7] introduces Distribution Matching Distillation for one-step image generation. These papers share the same objective at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves using Ryzhakov et al. (2024)'s explicit vector field formula to reverse-solve the Cauchy problem for target distribution samples, obtaining their prototypes, and training a neural network to directly map paired {prototype, target sample} data. The pairing method ensures nearly monotonic trajectories, and importance sampling is used for integral estimation. Papers [3], [5], [8], [13], and [26] describe similar mechanisms for rectifying or straightening flow paths in generative models to reduce truncation errors and improve sampling efficiency. For example, [3] discusses straightening probability flows for fast sampling, and [5] uses rectified flow to learn ODE paths connecting distributions. Additionally, [11] and [14] address solving inverse Cauchy problems using neural networks or numerical techniques, which aligns with the reverse-solving aspect of the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves qualitative demonstrations of one-step sampling on toy 2D datasets (e.g., 8 Gaussians) and MNIST, without quantitative metrics like FID. Papers [6], [7], [16], [17], and [26] use similar evaluation designs, such as qualitative demonstrations of one-step sampling on image datasets (e.g., MNIST or other benchmarks). For instance, [6] and [7] evaluate one-step generators on image synthesis tasks, and [16] applies Distribution Matching Distillation to unpaired image-to-image translation. The evaluation design (qualitative demonstration of sampling efficiency) is covered by these prior works.

### Domain
The domain is generative modeling, specifically fast sampling in Flow Matching. Papers [3], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [13], [16], [17], [22], and [26] all operate in the same general application area of generative modeling and fast sampling techniques for flow-based or diffusion models. For example, [3] focuses on fast sampling in continuous-time generative models, and [6] addresses efficient one-step generation in diffusion models. The domain is clearly covered.

## Purpose

The purpose is to eliminate the high computational cost of ODE solving in Flow Matching sampling, enabling one-step generation from initial to target distribution.

Papers [6], [7], [17], [26] all aim at one-step generation from diffusion models. Papers [3], [8], [9], [13] aim to reduce NFE in flow/diffusion models. Paper [5] (Rectified Flow) and [1] address straightening flows for faster sampling. The purpose of "one-step generation by eliminating ODE solving overhead" is substantively equivalent to papers like [6] ("Diffusion Models Are Innate One-Step Generators"), [7] (DMD: "one-step image generator"), [17] (EM Distillation for one-step), [26] (SiD: "single-step generator"). These all share the same objective: eliminate multi-step ODE/SDE sampling, achieve one-step generation.

## Mechanism

The mechanism involves: (1) using an explicit vector field formula (from Ryzhakov et al. 2024) to backward-solve a Cauchy problem for target samples to get their prototypes, (2) training a neural network on {prototype, target} pairs for direct mapping, (3) near-monotone trajectories (non-crossing), (4) importance sampling for integral estimation.

Paper [6] uses instance-based distillation pairing noise→data. Paper [5] uses reflow (pairing ODE-solved endpoints). Paper [1] also uses reflow-style pairing. The backward-solving via explicit vector field formula to find prototypes is a specific mechanism. Paper [5]'s "reflow" is the closest: solve ODE forward to get paired (x0, x1) then train directly — this is structurally similar (pair initial noise with target via ODE trajectory, train direct map). However, the contribution here reverses the direction (backward from target to find prototype) using an explicit formula rather than numerical ODE integration, and uses importance sampling. Paper [3] (Sequential Flow Straightening) also creates pairs by solving ODEs. The core primitive of "solve ODE to get paired endpoints, train direct neural map" is present in [5] and [3]. The importance sampling aspect appears in [20] (Gaussian-mixture umbrella sampling) but in a different context. The backward Cauchy problem solving is referenced in [11], [14], [25] but not in the flow matching context. The combination is somewhat novel, but the core pairing-then-direct-mapping primitive is covered by [5].

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses toy 2D (8 Gaussians) and MNIST with qualitative visualization, no FID. Paper [5] uses toy 2D experiments including Gaussian mixtures for qualitative evaluation. Paper [3] also uses toy 2D experiments. Paper [13] uses similar setups. The evaluation design (toy 2D Gaussian mixture + MNIST qualitative) is a standard design used in flow matching papers. Paper [5] explicitly uses multi-Gaussian toy experiments and image generation qualitative results. This design is covered.

## Domain

The domain is generative modeling / fast sampling in Flow Matching. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], [8], [12], [13] all work in generative modeling with flow matching. This is clearly covered.
